headline: US data center gas power demand doubles to 189 GW in under a year, research shows
summary: New research reveals US data centers' planned gas-fired power capacity has surged to over 189 gigawatts, nearly doubling in less than a year. This rapid expansion highlights tech companies' reliance on fossil fuels to meet AI's growing energy demands.
details: New research from Global Energy Monitor indicates that the amount of gas-fired power in development for US data centers has nearly doubled in less than a year. The demand pipeline has jumped to more than 189 gigawatts as of mid-2026, a massive increase from 97 gigawatts at the end of 2025.

This surge illustrates how heavily tech companies are relying on building private fossil fuel plants to power data centers, often bypassing lengthy grid connection times. This approach also aims to avoid burdening ratepayers with higher bills, a growing point of contention.

The Trump administration has encouraged this trend, with a voluntary pledge signed by major tech companies like Microsoft, Meta, Google, and OpenAI. However, adding this much natural gas power comes with a significant climate cost, particularly as many facilities use inefficient turbines that increase emissions.

The US has now surpassed China in gas projects for data centers, according to Global Energy Monitor. In contrast, China's data center boom is largely oriented around renewables, with many facilities sited in rural areas with excess solar and hydropower.

Experts note that while gas power might make economic sense in the near term for rapid data center deployment in the US, it incurs long-term costs in terms of emissions and a lack of investment in clean energy. Not all tracked projects are guaranteed to be built, but if they are, emissions will be locked in for decades.

headline_marked: [[Thomson Reuters launches 'Thomson']] its own proprietary frontier AI model
headline: Thomson Reuters launches 'Thomson' its own proprietary frontier AI model
summary: Thomson Reuters invested $40 million to train 'Thomson', its first proprietary large language model. This in-house model was developed at a fraction of the cost of typical frontier models and remains fully controlled by the company.
details: Thomson Reuters has launched 'Thomson', its first proprietary large language model, developed in-house. The company invested $40 million in its training, a significantly lower cost compared to the billions typically spent on comparable frontier models.

The new model, announced on August 24, 2026, is fully owned and controlled by Thomson Reuters, eliminating the heavy inference costs often associated with third-party frontier models. This approach emphasizes efficiency and specialized intelligence over sheer scale.

Thomson was built on decades of proprietary content, technology, and domain expertise from sources like Westlaw, Practical Law, Checkpoint, and Reuters. It was developed to Fiduciary-Grade™ standards, leveraging hundreds of subject matter experts.

Joel Hron, CTO of Thomson Reuters, stated that the company's approach demonstrates an alternative path to AI development. He highlighted that starting with a strong open-source foundation and specializing it deeply can create highly capable and efficient intelligence.

CEO Steve Hasker noted that Thomson's performance, based on early evaluations, is on par with the latest frontier models across various tasks. He emphasized the unique advantage of building AI on proprietary content and editorial expertise.

The AI is designed to streamline legal work, tax compliance, and trade operations. It offers features like AI-driven research workflows, automated HS code classification, and tools for legal research and drafting, aiming to reduce review times from hours to minutes.
